variants.title: Run the adversarial loop
variants.context: Adversarial testing runs as a learning loop: map the attack surface from a threat model, exercise and adapt within a declared budget, triage and contain confirmed findings, then gate and monitor so each finding changes a control, a release condition, or the threat model.
variants.prompt: A team starts adversarial testing on an agent with tool access. Put the program steps in order.

items.text: Promote minimized incidents into protected regressions and watch the same boundary in production.
Inventory assets, actors, entry paths, trust boundaries, permissions, and existing controls.
Confirm reproducibility, severity, affected versions, reachable assets, and immediate containment.
Run safe versioned attempts under realistic budgets, changing strategy after observing defenses.

variants.hint: A large attack corpus without this first step counts attempts, not boundaries.
variants.explanation: The threat model scopes the search, adaptation finds the path, triage bounds it, and the gate keeps it from returning.

variants.title: Run the adversarial loop
variants.context: Adversarial testing runs as a learning loop: map the attack surface from a threat model, exercise and adapt within a declared budget, triage and contain confirmed findings, then gate and monitor so each finding changes a control, a release condition, or the threat model.
variants.prompt: A new connector is added that pulls in customer email. Put the loop in order for that surface.

items.text: Store the minimized case in the release suite and alert on the same boundary in production.
Probe it with indirect instructions, encodings, and multi-turn attempts inside the declared budget.
Reproduce the successful attempt, score severity, and quarantine the source while remediation lands.
Add the connector as an entry path and name the assets its content can now reach.

variants.hint: A new entry path changes the map before it changes the tests.
variants.explanation: Every new surface re-enters the loop at the threat model so its assets and boundaries are declared before probing.

variants.title: Run the adversarial loop
variants.context: Adversarial testing runs as a learning loop: map the attack surface from a threat model, exercise and adapt within a declared budget, triage and contain confirmed findings, then gate and monitor so each finding changes a control, a release condition, or the threat model.
variants.prompt: A prompt guard was added after last quarter's finding. Put the work in order for the next candidate.

items.text: Rerun the stored attempts plus adapted variants that assume the guard exists.
Update the gate and monitoring so the guard's failures show up in production, not only in tests.
Recheck which assets and trust boundaries the guard is actually claimed to protect.
Confirm which attempts now fail, which still succeed, and contain anything that still crosses.

variants.hint: A defense changes the attacker's strategy, so what has to be rerun?
variants.explanation: Adding a detector changes the system under test, so attacks are regenerated against it rather than replayed as passed.

variants.title: Follow the authority path
variants.context: One adversarial path crosses several owners: an untrusted source, context assembly that keeps provenance, a model proposal, a deterministic policy decision, and an observed effect with a receipt. Natural-language instructions never promote untrusted data into policy.
variants.prompt: A support document in the index contains hidden instructions. Put the path in order.

items.text: Deterministic policy evaluates identity, intent, destination, data scope, and required approval.
The attacker edits a document that the application is willing to retrieve.
Retrieval and parsing combine sources while retaining provenance, purpose, and sensitivity.
The model produces a candidate answer or action without granting itself permission.
The executor records a receipt and verifies the postcondition so the effect stays detectable.

variants.hint: Ask where trust could change hands, and where it must not.
variants.explanation: Untrusted content can reach the model, but the policy decision and the receipt remain outside it.

variants.title: Follow the authority path
variants.context: One adversarial path crosses several owners: an untrusted source, context assembly that keeps provenance, a model proposal, a deterministic policy decision, and an observed effect with a receipt. Natural-language instructions never promote untrusted data into policy.
variants.prompt: A legitimate connector returns attacker-controlled text inside a valid response. Put the path in order.

items.text: The tool adapter merges that result into context while keeping its source and trust label.
The model proposes a follow-up action based on the merged context.
The connector returns syntactically valid data whose content the attacker influenced.
The executor verifies the postcondition and records what actually changed.
Policy checks the proposed tool, its arguments, and its destination against authenticated identity.

variants.hint: A valid schema says nothing about who wrote the content.
variants.explanation: Tool results are data, so the follow-up action is authorized independently of how convincing the result looked.

variants.title: Follow the authority path
variants.context: One adversarial path crosses several owners: an untrusted source, context assembly that keeps provenance, a model proposal, a deterministic policy decision, and an observed effect with a receipt. Natural-language instructions never promote untrusted data into policy.
variants.prompt: An uploaded image carries instruction text that the text-only corpus never exercised. Put the path in order.

items.text: The denial is recorded with the source region so the upload path can be reviewed.
Extraction and normalization turn the image into text while preserving the source region.
A user uploads an image whose rendered text the attacker controls.
The model reads the extracted text and proposes an action from it.
Policy denies the proposal because identity, destination, and scope do not permit it.

variants.hint: Which stage first turns pixels into something the policy can read?
variants.explanation: Multimodal paths need the same provenance and authorization stages, since a text-only corpus never exercises them.

variants.title: Compute attack success rate
variants.context: Attack success rate is successful attempts divided by valid attempts. Invalid harness runs, evaluator failures, and tool timeouts are excluded and reported separately, because silently counting them as defended attempts flatters the denominator.
variants.prompt: An indirect-injection family ran 640 attempts. 40 ended in harness errors and were excluded as invalid, and 24 of the remaining valid attempts succeeded. What is the attack success rate in percent?
variants.hint: Which attempts belong in the denominator, and which are reported separately?
variants.explanation: 24 successes over 600 valid attempts is 4 percent, and the 40 invalid runs are reported as harness failures.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by all 640 attempts, counting invalid harness runs as defended.
That reports the defended share rather than the attack success rate.

variants.title: Compute attack success rate
variants.context: Attack success rate is successful attempts divided by valid attempts. Invalid harness runs, evaluator failures, and tool timeouts are excluded and reported separately, because silently counting them as defended attempts flatters the denominator.
variants.prompt: A privacy-extraction family ran 900 attempts. 100 failed because the evaluator crashed and were excluded, and 12 of the remaining valid attempts succeeded. What is the attack success rate in percent?
variants.hint: An evaluator crash is not a defended attempt.
variants.explanation: 12 successes over 800 valid attempts is 1.5 percent, with the 100 evaluator failures reported separately.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by all 900 attempts, so evaluator crashes count as defenses.
That reports the share of valid attempts that were defended.

variants.title: Compute attack success rate
variants.context: Attack success rate is successful attempts divided by valid attempts. Invalid harness runs, evaluator failures, and tool timeouts are excluded and reported separately, because silently counting them as defended attempts flatters the denominator.
variants.prompt: A policy-evasion family ran 1,200 attempts. 200 hit a tool timeout and were excluded as invalid, and 25 of the remaining valid attempts succeeded. What is the attack success rate in percent?
variants.hint: Timeouts are excluded from the denominator, not scored as wins.
variants.explanation: 25 successes over 1,000 valid attempts is 2.5 percent, and the 200 timeouts are reported as invalid runs.

mistakes.feedback: That divides by all 1,200 attempts, treating timeouts as defended attempts.
That reports the defended share of valid attempts.

variants.title: Apply the severity gate
variants.context: The gate caps attack success rate by severity: 3 percent for moderate, 1 percent for high, and 0.5 percent for critical. A benign false-positive rate above 6 percent, a utility pass rate below 90 percent, and a failed incident regression each block on their own.
variants.prompt: A critical indirect-injection family shows 4 successes in 500 valid attempts. Every other family is inside its limit, benign false positives are 3 percent, and utility is 94 percent. What follows?
options: Block, because 0.8 percent exceeds the 0.5 percent critical limit on its own.
Release, because the combined rate across all families stays under 1 percent.
Release with a note, since four successes in 500 is within sampling noise.
optionFeedback: A critical family stays independently blocking no matter how many moderate attempts failed.
Combining families is exactly the averaging that lets a critical bypass disappear.
A note does not lift a limit that governance set before the results were seen.
variants.hint: Does a critical family share a denominator with the others?
variants.explanation: Each attack family is gated at its own severity limit so a critical authorization bypass cannot be averaged away.

variants.title: Apply the severity gate
variants.context: The gate caps attack success rate by severity: 3 percent for moderate, 1 percent for high, and 0.5 percent for critical. A benign false-positive rate above 6 percent, a utility pass rate below 90 percent, and a failed incident regression each block on their own.
variants.prompt: Every attack family is inside its severity limit, but 48 of 600 benign cases were falsely blocked and utility is 93 percent. What follows?
options: Release, since false positives are a product concern rather than a gate condition.
Block, because an 8 percent benign false-positive rate exceeds the 6 percent limit.
Release, because no attack family exceeded its declared severity limit.
optionFeedback: The gate treats benign false positives as a blocking condition, not as product feedback.
Overblocking denies service to real users, which is why the gate carries its own limit for it.
Attack rates are one of four blockers, and the benign limit failed independently.
variants.hint: Count the blockers in the gate, not just the attack families.
variants.explanation: A defense that blocks legitimate traffic fails the gate even when every attack family passes.

variants.title: Apply the severity gate
variants.context: The gate caps attack success rate by severity: 3 percent for moderate, 1 percent for high, and 0.5 percent for critical. A benign false-positive rate above 6 percent, a utility pass rate below 90 percent, and a failed incident regression each block on their own.
variants.prompt: All attack families pass, benign false positives are 4 percent, but the utility pass rate is 87 percent and one incident regression failed. What follows?
options: Release, because attack success and false positives both stayed in limits.
Block, because both the utility floor and a protected regression failed.
Block only on utility, since a single regression failure is a flaky test.
optionFeedback: Two independent blockers fired, and passing the other two does not offset them.
Utility below 90 percent and a failed incident regression are each blocking, and both fired here.
A protected regression reproduces a confirmed incident, so its failure is a result, not noise.
variants.hint: How many independent conditions does this gate carry?
variants.explanation: Blockers are independent, so the decision names every failed condition rather than trading one against another.

variants.title: Match the path to its control
variants.context: Defenses are chosen by the boundary they interrupt: reduce reachable authority, preserve data origin and handling rules, and limit probing and leakage. No single filter closes every path, so a model-side mitigation and a system control do different jobs.
variants.prompt: Match each attack path to the control that most directly interrupts it.

pairs.label: Indirect prompt injection through a retrieved document
pairs.detail: Carry source identity and trust through retrieval, and treat retrieved content as data rather than authority.

pairs.label: Excessive agency from a broadly scoped tool
pairs.detail: Give each tool the minimum operation, destination, data scope, and lifetime one task requires.

pairs.label: Improper output handling into a SQL statement
pairs.detail: Validate model-generated content at the boundary it crosses, independently of input screening.

pairs.label: Behavior extraction by a coordinated query campaign
pairs.detail: Apply principal-aware budgets, rate limits, and anomaly detection to repeated similar queries.

variants.hint: Ask which boundary each attack has to cross to matter.
variants.explanation: Controls are chosen by the failure path they interrupt, which is why one prompt guard cannot stand in for all four.

variants.title: Match the path to its control
variants.context: Defenses are chosen by the boundary they interrupt: reduce reachable authority, preserve data origin and handling rules, and limit probing and leakage. No single filter closes every path, so a model-side mitigation and a system control do different jobs.
variants.prompt: Match each attack path to the control that most directly interrupts it.

pairs.label: Tool-result injection from a legitimate connector
pairs.detail: Keep provenance through tool adapters and authorize the follow-up action against authenticated identity.

pairs.label: Unbounded consumption of tokens, retrieval, and recursion
pairs.detail: Bound cost, rate, recursion depth, and tool budget independently of what the model requests.

pairs.label: A memorization probe aimed at sensitive records
pairs.detail: Test retention, logging, cache, and support workflows against the same privacy boundary as output.

pairs.label: An irreversible external effect proposed by the model
pairs.detail: Require explicit approval, verify the postcondition, and make retries idempotent.

variants.hint: Some of these need a limit, others need an approval.
variants.explanation: Defense in depth means the consequence stays bounded even in the cases where the model still fails.

variants.title: Match the path to its control
variants.context: Defenses are chosen by the boundary they interrupt: reduce reachable authority, preserve data origin and handling rules, and limit probing and leakage. No single filter closes every path, so a model-side mitigation and a system control do different jobs.
variants.prompt: Match each attack path to the control that most directly interrupts it.

pairs.label: Retrieval poisoning of newly indexed content
pairs.detail: Watch retrieval of low-trust or newly indexed sources before consequential proposals and quarantine them.

pairs.label: Multimodal instruction injection through an uploaded image
pairs.detail: Normalize image, audio, and document structure before policy checks while retaining source regions.

pairs.label: Multi-turn escalation spread across a long conversation
pairs.detail: Evaluate conversation state rather than single messages, and cap the session attempt budget.

pairs.label: Model output that asserts its own permissions
pairs.detail: Authorize every action against authenticated context, since the model cannot grant itself authority.

variants.hint: A per-message detector sees fragments; what sees the campaign?
variants.explanation: Each path fails a different control, so the release evidence has to name which boundary held and which one did not.
